quiz.q: What does 'inflation' do to money you keep idle?
o: Reduces what it can buy over time
quiz.w: Prices rise over time, so the same amount buys less. Idle cash loses buying power quietly.

quiz.q: Which is a 'need'?
quiz.w: Needs keep you safe and functioning. Wants improve life but can wait.

quiz.q: A simple way to see where money goes is to…
o: Track spending for a few weeks
quiz.w: A few weeks of tracking beats memory. Small items add up more than we expect.

quiz.q: A 'real' return is…
quiz.w: Real return subtracts inflation. 7% growth with 5% inflation is roughly 2% real.

quiz.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
o: Move savings out right after income arrives
quiz.w: Saving first, spending what's left, flips the usual order and builds the habit.

quiz.q: How big is a common emergency-fund target?
quiz.w: 3–6 months of essential expenses is a common guide; more if income is uneven.

quiz.q: In the 50/30/20 idea, the 20 usually stands for…
quiz.w: It's a starting frame: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and extra debt payment.

quiz.q: Where should emergency money mainly prioritise?
quiz.w: You need it when something goes wrong. Availability and safety beat return.

quiz.q: Your savings rate is best defined as…
quiz.w: Savings rate = the share of income you keep. It matters more than any single return.

quiz.q: What is diversification?
quiz.w: Different assets behave differently. Spreading reduces the damage from any one.

quiz.q: Which usually goes with higher potential return?
quiz.w: Higher potential return usually means higher uncertainty. Nothing offers both for free.

quiz.q: A SIP invests…
o: A fixed amount at regular intervals
quiz.w: Regular investing smooths your entry price and builds the habit.

quiz.q: Longer time horizon generally allows…
o: More capacity to ride out ups and downs
quiz.w: More time gives short-term swings room to even out. It never guarantees outcomes.

quiz.q: If a portfolio falls 50%, what gain is needed to recover?
quiz.w: ₹100 → ₹50 needs to double back to ₹100, a 100% gain. Drawdowns hurt more than they look.

quiz.q: What is 'rebalancing'?
o: Restoring your target mix after drift
quiz.w: Rebalancing trims what grew and tops up what lagged to return to your intended risk.

quiz.q: Which debt usually costs the most interest?
quiz.w: Unpaid card balances typically carry the highest rates. Pay in full when you can.

quiz.q: A sensible EMI-to-income comfort zone is often…
quiz.w: Keeping total EMIs under roughly 40% of income leaves room for life and savings.

quiz.q: Paying only the minimum due on a card…
o: Keeps interest running on the rest
quiz.w: Minimum payments keep you in debt longer. Interest accrues on the remaining balance.

quiz.q: The 'avalanche' repayment method targets…
quiz.w: Avalanche saves the most interest. 'Snowball' (smallest first) trades savings for motivation.

quiz.q: What is insurance mainly for?
o: Transferring a big risk you can't absorb
quiz.w: Insurance covers rare, large losses. Treat it as protection, not an investment.

quiz.q: Term insurance is most relevant when…
quiz.w: It replaces income for dependants if you're gone. Cover should reflect loans and goals.

quiz.q: Health cover from work alone is…
o: Worth supplementing since it may end with the job
quiz.w: Employer cover can end when the job does. A personal base policy adds continuity.

quiz.q: A common rule of thumb for term cover is…
o: About 10–15× annual income, adjusted for your situation
quiz.w: It's a starting point only. Loans, dependants and goals shift the real number.

quiz.q: Compounding means…
quiz.w: Returns earned begin to earn their own returns. Time is the main ingredient.

quiz.q: Which habit best beats lifestyle creep?
quiz.w: Give each raise a job: send part straight to savings before spending expands.

quiz.q: Which is true of any investment?
o: Value can go up and down
quiz.w: Values move. Past performance doesn't guarantee what comes next.

cards.b: Before a non-essential purchase, wait a day. If you still want it tomorrow, it's a considered choice, not an impulse.
cards.try: Try it on your next 'quick buy'.

cards.b: Divide 72 by an annual return rate to estimate years to double. At 8%, about 9 years. It's an approximation, not a promise.
A 40% card balance outruns almost any savings return. Clearing high-interest debt is a guaranteed 'return'.
cards.try: List your debts by interest rate.

cards.b: Missing a handful of the best market days can hurt a lot, but they often sit next to the worst days. Staying invested avoids guessing.
Savings with a name ('Goa trip') are protected better than savings with none. Labels make dipping in feel real.
cards.try: Rename one account or pot today.

cards.b: Mixing protection and investment in one product can make both worse. Often it's clearer to keep them separate.
cards.try: Check what each policy is for.

cards.b: Add a third bucket to needs and wants: future-you. Pay it first, so it never competes with wants.
Risk is also not meeting your goal: too little growth, or panic-selling at the wrong time.
cards.try: Ask: what's my real risk here?

cards.t: Credit score is a habit report
cards.b: On-time payments and low utilisation shape your credit history. Both are habits you can improve.
cards.try: Set a reminder for due dates.

cards.b: Raise your savings by half of every raise. You still feel better off, and goals speed up.
Assets minus liabilities. It's a single number that shows direction. Watch it quarterly, not daily.
A small yearly fee shrinks the base that grows. Over decades, a 1% difference can be large.
cards.try: Find the cost of one product you hold.

cards.b: Money you need within 2–3 years generally shouldn't ride on market swings. Long goals can accept some.
Annual bills (insurance, gifts, repairs) are predictable. Save 1/12th each month into a pot so they stop being 'emergencies'.
Tracking, automating and reviewing weekly will do more than any clever trick. Boring works.

spin.l: Money grows on its own growth. ₹10,000 at 8% becomes about ₹21,600 in 10 years if returns stay steady (illustrative).
spin.w: Time is the key ingredient. Starting early beats starting big.

spin.l: A pot of 3–6 months of essentials, kept accessible and separate from spending.
spin.w: It exists to be there fast when life surprises you.

spin.l: Paying the full card bill by the due date avoids interest and builds history.
spin.w: Full, on-time payment is free borrowing with no interest.

spin.l: If prices rise 6% a year, ₹100 buys what ₹94 does after a year.
spin.w: Over time, rising prices erode purchasing power.

spin.l: Different assets move differently. A mix makes the ride steadier.
spin.w: It reduces the damage from any single surprise.

spin.l: Investing a fixed amount regularly buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high.
spin.w: It automates discipline and averages your entry over time.

spin.l: Insurance moves rare, large losses off your own balance sheet.
spin.w: Keep protection and investing separate for clarity.

spin.l: A budget is a plan for your money, not a punishment. 50/30/20 is one starting frame.
spin.w: It gives each rupee a purpose before the month starts.

spin.l: Taxes shape what you keep. Knowing your slab and eligible savings avenues is part of planning (check current rules).
spin.q: Planning for taxes is best done…
spin.w: Spread planning avoids the last-minute rush and bad choices.

spin.l: Group goals by horizon: under 3 years, 3–7, 7+. Each deserves a different risk level.
spin.w: Timelines decide the risk your money can afford.

journey.d: What money is for, and how it works.

steps.b: Money isn't the goal; what it lets you do is. Start by naming what you want your money to do for you in 5 years.
steps.q: A good first step in money planning is…
o: Know what you want it to do

steps.b: Income minus spending leaves saving, but flip it: decide saving first, then spend the rest.
steps.w: Setting savings aside first protects it.

journey.d: A simple plan you'll actually follow.

steps.b: Roughly 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and extra debt payments. Adjust for your life; the point is the conversation.
steps.w: It's the part that builds your future.

steps.b: Track three weeks of spending, find the leak that surprises you, and fix just that one first.
steps.w: One change you keep beats ten you drop.

journey.d: Emergency funds and why they come first.

steps.b: Surprises are normal: medical bills, repairs, job gaps. A buffer keeps them from becoming debt.
steps.q: Without a buffer, surprises often become…
steps.w: Borrowing at high interest is the usual result.

steps.b: Aim for 3–6 months of essentials in an easy-to-access, low-risk place. Build it in steps: 1 month first.
steps.q: Where does an emergency fund belong?

steps.b: Debt is a tool with a price. Compare interest rate, purpose and your ability to repay. Cards left unpaid are the costliest.
steps.w: Revolving card interest is typically highest.

steps.b: Avalanche pays highest rate first and saves most interest; snowball pays smallest first and builds momentum.
Higher potential returns come with higher uncertainty. Nothing in investing is both guaranteed and high.
steps.w: Be suspicious of anything promising both.

steps.b: Spread across assets, match to your timeline and invest regularly. Avoid reacting to every headline.

journey.d: Match money to the time you have.

steps.b: Every goal needs a name, a rupee target and a date. Without all three it's a wish.
Money needed in under 3 years prefers stability; long-term goals can handle growth-oriented risk.
steps.q: A goal due in 18 months prefers…
steps.w: Little time means little room to recover from a fall.

steps.b: Insurance is for losses you can't absorb: health emergencies, loss of income, major liabilities.
steps.w: Pay a small premium to avoid a ruinous cost.

steps.b: Term cover should reflect dependants, loans and goals. Review after big life events.
steps.w: Marriage, kids, loans change the number.

thu-beginner.title: The unexpected ₹10,000
thu-beginner.setup: A relative gifts you ₹10,000 out of the blue. You have almost no savings. What do you do?

opts.t: Spend it all on that new gadget
opts.f: Understandable, but you'd start from zero again. A gift is a rare chance to build a buffer.

opts.t: Put ₹7,000 in your emergency pot, enjoy ₹3,000
opts.f: Balanced. You build safety and still feel the win, which makes the habit sustainable.

opts.t: Put all ₹10,000 into a high-risk investment
opts.f: Building a cushion usually comes before taking risk. A fall here could leave you with nothing to fall back on.

thu-beginner.lesson: Windfalls are best split: mostly to your future, a little for joy.

thu-young.title: The raise decision
thu-young.setup: You've received a 15% raise. Your rent and subscriptions already feel tight. What's your move?

opts.t: Upgrade lifestyle: new flat, new phone
opts.f: Lifestyle creep absorbs raises quietly. Joy is fine, but nothing is left for goals.

opts.t: Auto-send half of the raise to savings, enjoy the rest
opts.f: This is the habit the best savers share. You still feel richer, and goals accelerate.

opts.t: Save the whole raise, cut all fun
opts.f: Admirable, but a plan without joy is hard to sustain. Aim for a rule you can keep.

thu-young.lesson: Give every raise a job before it becomes spending.

thu-investor.title: The hot sector
thu-investor.setup: A sector is up 60% this year and everyone talks about it. Your simulated portfolio is already above target equity. What do you do?

opts.t: Add more to catch the momentum
opts.f: That's recency bias. Chasing winners often means buying after the rise.
A rule made in calm times beats a decision made in excitement. That's what process means.

opts.t: Sell everything and wait for a fall
opts.f: Timing both exits and entries is very hard. Large moves based on feeling tend to cost more.

thu-investor.lesson: A rule written in calm protects you in noise. (Simulated discussion, not advice.)

thu-family.title: The school fee surprise
thu-family.setup: A school fee jumps by ₹40,000 this term, due in 3 weeks. You have a home loan EMI and some savings. What first?

opts.t: Put it on a credit card and pay minimums
opts.f: Minimum payments let interest run and strain an already loaded budget.

opts.t: Use the sinking-fund pot for annual costs, then top it up monthly
opts.f: Planned pots stop predictable costs from becoming crises. Rebuild it so it's ready next time.
That trades a short-term gap for a long-term hole. Look at planned pots and cash flow first.

thu-family.lesson: Name predictable costs, then fund them monthly.

thu-saver.title: The idle goal money
thu-saver.setup: Your home down payment is due in 2 years. A friend says to put it in a high-return, high-risk fund to get there faster. What do you do?

opts.t: Go all in on the risky fund
opts.f: A fall close to the due date can't be recovered in time. Time horizon matters more than return chasing.

opts.t: Keep it in stable, accessible options matched to the date
opts.f: Short timelines favour stability. Your discipline does the heavy lifting here.

opts.t: Leave it in a plain account earning nothing
opts.f: Safe, but idle cash loses to inflation. Stable options that earn something are a middle path.

thu-saver.lesson: Match risk to the date of the goal, not to the hope for it.

savingsRounds.d: Colleagues are ordering in. Your share is
A flash sale on something you didn't need
A subscription you barely use costs per month
A cab to a spot reachable by metro
Payday! Move a portion to goals first

qs.q: A surprise bonus arrives. First instinct?
o: Plan how it supports my goals
Look for something to grow it

qs.q: A friend offers a 'hot tip'. You…
o: Ask how it fits my plan

types.d: You like plans and progress. You finish what you start and trust the process.
types.tip: Add one small learning goal each month to widen your toolkit.

types.d: You're curious and comfortable with uncertainty. You look for opportunity.
types.tip: Write a rule for when you stop, and size positions to survive being wrong.

types.d: You value safety and stability. You prepare for rainy days.
types.tip: Review whether long-term money is beating inflation.

types.d: You value experiences now. You're generous and spontaneous.
types.tip: Automate 'future-you' first so enjoying today stays guilt-free.

scenarios.d: A bad first year, then a rebound.
A lot of noise, little progress.
Unlocks at level 3. Long, painful drag.

healthChecks.yes: Great. Awareness is the base of control.
healthChecks.no: A quick scan of your last 5 transactions is a fine start.

healthChecks.q: Are your upcoming bills and EMIs covered?
healthChecks.no: List the next three due dates and set reminders today.

healthChecks.q: Did you set money aside before spending?
healthChecks.yes: Paying yourself first is the strongest habit.
healthChecks.no: Try moving a small fixed amount on payday.

healthChecks.q: Do you know your safety-net size?
healthChecks.yes: Knowing it is half of building it.
healthChecks.no: Divide your savings by your monthly essentials to find out.
